questions.prompt: Which statement reads data without changing it?
questions.explanation: SELECT only reads. Testers verifying data should mostly use SELECT, ideally with a read-only account.
ORDER BY sorts. Without it, row order is not guaranteed, so tests must not depend on it.

questions.prompt: `WHERE name LIKE 'A%'` matches names that start with A.
questions.explanation: `%` matches any sequence of characters, so 'A%' means 'starts with A'. Case sensitivity depends on the database and collation.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson-style customers table (Asha Pune, Ben Mumbai, Chen Pune, Dana NULL city), how many rows does this return?
questions.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Pune');
questions.explanation: IN ('Pune') matches Asha and Chen. Dana's NULL city is not equal to anything, so she is not returned by IN or by NOT IN.

questions.prompt: Which query safely checks how many rows an UPDATE will affect before you run it in a test environment?
options: A SELECT COUNT(*) with the same WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Running the same WHERE as a SELECT first shows exactly which rows would change. Better still, do the change inside a transaction you can roll back.

questions.prompt: Which are good habits for testers writing SQL against shared test databases? Select all that apply.
options: Use explicit column lists instead of SELECT * in automated checks
Filter by the ids your test created
Use LIMIT when exploring large tables
Run UPDATE without WHERE to reset data quickly
questions.explanation: Explicit columns resist schema additions, id filters isolate tests, and LIMIT protects shared databases. An UPDATE without WHERE changes every row.

questions.prompt: This check should find customers without a city, but returns no rows although Dana has a NULL city. Why?
questions.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = NULL;
options: Comparisons with NULL using = are never true; use IS NULL
Empty string and NULL are the same
questions.explanation: NULL means unknown, so `city = NULL` evaluates to unknown and filters the row out. `city IS NULL` is the correct test. (Some data may also use '' and needs a separate check.)

questions.prompt: A tester verifies a bug fix by running `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'Paid'` and gets zero rows, then reports the fix as broken. The data uses lower-case 'paid'. What lesson applies?
options: Check the actual stored values (e.g. SELECT DISTINCT status) before writing assertions; string comparison can be case-sensitive
questions.explanation: Know your data: DISTINCT reveals the real values and their case. Whether '=' is case-sensitive depends on the database and collation.

coding.title: Filter and sort orders
coding.prompt:
List `id` and `amount` of **paid** orders with an amount of at least 100, highest amount first.

Expected: `103 | 300.0`, `101 | 120.0`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 100 ORDER BY amount DESC;
coding.explanation: Combine conditions with AND in WHERE, then ORDER BY ... DESC. `>=` includes the boundary value 100.

coding.title: Customers with no city
coding.prompt:
Data-quality check: list `name` of customers whose `city` is missing (NULL or an empty string), ordered by name.

Expected: Dana.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL OR city = '' ORDER BY name;
coding.explanation: IS NULL catches real NULLs; the `= ''` branch catches empty strings that some imports produce. Testing both is a good habit.
